This report provides an update on the city's investment income forecast for 2026 and 2027.
As well as addresses the direction provided by committee at the April 8th, 2026 standing policy committee on finance meeting.

As outlined in the report, the city's approach to budgeting and utilizing investment income has changed significantly since introducing equities and alternative investments into the city's investment portfolio.
The city's approach now includes providing an operating budget contribution as general revenues to support core services and reduce property tax requirements.
And in 2026, this is set at 17.63 million and is to be provided regardless of how the city's investment portfolio performs.
Any remaining surplus or deficit that is actually realized in the city's investment portfolio is provided to or from the investment income reserve.

The amount provided for the operating budget is generally recommended to be conservative as this allows for fluctuations in the city's investment earnings and the investment income to be a source of capital funding in the future.
On 2025's net investment earnings forecast of 25.73 million and potentially up to 32 million in 2026.
There's likely room to adjust the city's operating budget investment income in 2027 while continuing to be conservative.

As such, the administration is currently working on the 2027 budget update and as part of that will be recommending an increase to the city's investment income amount which is included in the operating budget.

And increase like this could be used for a variety of reasons including reducing budgetary risk in other areas we know have been overstated such as franchise fees, grants and lose or other general revenues.
Enhancing service levels or programs through an expenditure increase or reducing the 2027 property tax requirement.
At this point, the administration is likely to recommend a combination of these adjustments and will be presented for decision at budget deliberations.
The report at this time is recommended to be received as information, but administration will be happy to answer any questions.

Next slide, please. So to start off, I would like to take a bit of time to share a summary of what my property is.
In a nutshell, my property is a secure online self-service portal for residents who prefer digital access to delivery of their utility assessment and property tax notices.
It is a convenient, easy to use portal that allows for customers to access current and pass notices and it's all in one place.
It's an optional service, meaning no one will be required to use it, but it does come at no cost of the customer.
We anticipate launching my property in early October, but the course that is contingent on the continued success of our user acceptance testing, which is currently ongoing.

I did want to also take a bit of time to talk about the design and the key principles that went into the design of the service. Excuse me.
You know, one of the key focuses for us was to ensure that the technology used provides customers with a secure platform review their data.

This includes an emphasis on cybersecurity protection and encryption. Another design philosophy was to ensure it will work on all commonly used modern browsers and commonly used expected devices like desktop, laptops, tablets, mobile phones etc.
In all cases, my property does use data pulled directly from CIS, which is the city's current billing system.

So this will allow customers to have up to data access to the information that the city uses just as if they were to contact a customer service representative in corporate revenue. Next slide, please.
So the good news for folks like me is signing up for my property is very simple and quick, especially if you're an existing customer.
All existing customers will be have been provided a unique access code. These were provided over the last few months on utility bills, assessment notices and property tax notices.

Setting up for the account is just a few clicks of a button and essentially links your individual customer number to that access code and allows for the information in CIS to then flow through to the portal.
New customers, however, will be able to also sign up for my property during account setup, or once they've been entered into the system.
A good example of that would be those customers that sign up through express address. It's a very common tool.
Those folks will be able to sign up for my property once we process their entry into CIS.

So I want to talk a little bit about the benefits for the customers. Why switch over? What's the point?

So benefits to the city. There are several as well.

Obvious one, paper and mailing cost savings. I can't provide you an exact figure today, but just for some context each customer that switches from paper to electronic notice for a utility bill would save the city $1.75 per month.
Whereas assessment and property tax would be about $2 per notice.
The reason there's a slight difference is assessment and property tax notices tend to be additional pages, so there's a little bit of an increased cost in the printing mailing is the same.
